concept.name: Status quo bias
concept.definition: A preference for maintaining the current state of affairs, such that an option is disproportionately favored when it is designated as the status quo or default. Documented by Samuelson and Zeckhauser (1988), it is linked to loss aversion, regret avoidance, and the endowment effect, and is distinct from a rational preference for the current state.
concept.intuition: Whatever allocation or position you already have feels safer than any change, so portfolios drift and stale positions linger.
concept.mechanics: In choice experiments, labeling an option as the status quo significantly raises the share choosing it, and the effect grows with the number of alternatives; real-world defaults (retirement-plan enrollment, the New Jersey versus Pennsylvania auto-insurance natural experiment) produced large participation differences. Switching away is coded as a risky loss relative to the reference state.
concept.failure_modes: It can be rational under transaction costs, information limits, or genuinely superior current states, so observed inertia is not automatically bias. It also interacts with omission bias, making the two hard to separate empirically.
concept.misconceptions: Status quo bias is not laziness alone, and loss aversion does not fully explain it - the bias appears even without gain/loss framing. In trading, doing nothing is itself a decision with risk consequences.
concept.example: A trader keeps a stale position and outdated stop levels for months because changing them feels like an active risk, while an identical fresh setup would never pass his entry rules.
